entry.evidence: However, no previous studies have investigated how wave activity can lead to changes in PM 2.5 concentrations

steps.action: The authors pose whether and how surface PM2.5 relates to the atmospheric general circulation, a question they say prior meteorology–PM2.5 studies leave open.
steps.quote: questions remain regarding whether and how PM 2.5 concentrations directly related to atmospheric general circulation

steps.action: They take over the anticyclonic wave activity (AWA) diagnostic and the regression and projection approach from co-authors' earlier ozone work (Sun et al. 2019; Chen et al. 2015) and compute AWA from 500 hPa geopotential height; they also add quantile regression.
steps.quote: This study is a followup study to Sun et al. (2019), using the same approach used there to analyze ozone

steps.action: They assemble summer IMPROVE PM2.5 at 150 stations (1988–2014) and ERA-Interim 500 hPa heights, then detrend and deseasonalize both series to isolate synoptic variability.
steps.quote: All stations with at least 1000 valid PM 2.5 values between 1988 and 2014 are collected in this study, totaling 150 stations

steps.action: They use existing CCMI CESM CAM4-Chem runs: reanalysis-driven REFC1SD, coupled GCM2000 and GCM2100 with current emissions, and REFC2 with future emissions.
steps.quote: We compare the IMPROVE data with output from the Community Earth System Model (CESM) as simulated for the Chemistry-Climate Model Initiative (CCMI)

steps.action: They check simulated monthly climatologies of PM2.5 against observations at the three representative sites (r > 0.80).
steps.quote: A statistically significant correlation ( r > 0.80 , p < 0.01 ; Fig. 2) for current PM 2.5 is found between observations and simulations

steps.action: They describe the simulated mean AWA and PM2.5 fields and their differences across the current and future scenarios.
steps.quote: There is an increase in PM 2.5 concentration for the future scenario with current emissions (GCM2100), while there is a decrease

steps.action: They regress daily deseasonalized PM2.5 at AREN1, SIPS1 and LAVO1 on AWA at every grid point and find positive coefficients near the sites.
steps.quote: the PM 2.5 concentrations are positively correlated with AWA in the areas close to the sites

steps.action: They repeat the regression with model-simulated PM2.5 (REFC1SD, GCM2000) and find that the reanalysis-driven run reproduces the observed pattern while the coupled run does less well.
steps.quote: Overall the model simulates similar spatial patterns to the observations for the case of the reanalysis-driven simulations (REFC1SD) but does less well

steps.action: They compute composites of AWA on days above the 90th percentile of PM2.5 as a second method, choosing the threshold after comparing quantiles (Fig. S1), and find patterns similar to the regression.
steps.quote: The composite AWA calculated by averaging together all AWA corresponding to daily PM 2.5 above the 90th quantile shows a similar strong connection

steps.action: They extend the composite and regression maxima to every station and grid point for all five data combinations and find a positive link across the US with regional differences.
steps.quote: PM 2.5 concentrations are positively correlated with AWA throughout the US but with varying strengths

steps.action: They propose that the link works through anticyclonic conditions: subsidence, light wind, no rain and inversions.
steps.quote: which is likely accounted for by arid weather and sinking inversions

steps.action: They set the result beside published stagnation–PM2.5 and stagnation–ozone studies and report consistency.
steps.quote: This is consistent with the PM 2.5 sensitivity study of Tai et al. ( [...] ).

steps.action: They fit linear and quantile regressions (10th to 90th percentiles) of AREN1 PM2.5 on AWA averaged over an impact region and find the 90th percentile about three times as sensitive as the 10th, with an overall r of only 0.36.
steps.quote: the 90th percentile of PM 2.5 is approximately 3 times more sensitive to the averaged AWA over the impact region

steps.action: They test whether the larger high-quantile sensitivity holds at all 150 sites by differencing the 90th- and 50th-percentile slopes.
steps.quote: Out of the 150 sites, 145 sites show that 90th-percentile PM 2.5 increases more than the 50th percentile

steps.action: They compare the quantile result with Porter et al. (2015) quantile-regression sensitivities to temperature.
steps.quote: These results are to some extent consistent with those from Porter et al. (2015)

steps.action: In GCM2000 they regress interannual PM2.5 on the projection of AWA anomalies onto the regression pattern and map the explained variance (R² from 0 to 0.75).
steps.quote: the projected value (using only AWA changes) captures up to 75 % of the interannual variability in PM 2.5

steps.action: They extrapolate the present-day linear relation, assumed stationary, to predict future PM2.5 change from the GCM2100 minus GCM2000 AWA change.
steps.quote: future PM 2.5 changes can be estimated by using the linear relationship fitted with the current data and projected change in AWA

steps.action: They compare the AWA-predicted change with the total simulated change as a fraction (Fig. 10); the fraction is highest in the western US.
steps.quote: the fraction of predicted JJA PM 2.5 change in total JJA PM 2.5 change from the simulation is calculated in Fig. 10

steps.action: They examine the simulated future change in 500 hPa height (Fig. S2) as the circulation change behind the AWA change.
steps.quote: The 500 hPa geopotential height increases everywhere by approximately 25–55 m over the entire US.

steps.action: They compare the projected future PM2.5 change with published projections, some agreeing and some contrary, and attribute the differences to model formulation.
steps.quote: The discrepancy between studies mentioned above and the results given here is most likely attributable to differences in model formulation.

steps.action: They note that the AWA-predicted change differs from the simulated change (largest in the east) and attribute this to the AWA change pattern and to meteorological drivers the univariate linear model omits, rather than revising the PM2.5–AWA claim.
steps.quote: This discrepancy mostly results from the distribution of projected AWA change (Fig. 3).

steps.action: They keep the claim that summer PM2.5 is positively linked to local AWA, that high percentiles are more sensitive, and that models and observations agree in general pattern.
steps.quote: PM 2.5 is positively linked to the local anticyclonic finite-amplitude wave activity over the past 2 decades during JJA

tree.answer: A possible PM2.5–AWA link, expected by analogy with the ozone–wave activity correlation; no anomaly
PM2.5 is observed directly (IMPROVE); AWA is a diagnostic computed from reanalysis Z500
Quantify the PM2.5–AWA relation and its quantile sensitivity, then use it to project future change
No stated rival hypotheses; emissions and other meteorological drivers are acknowledged but not tested
No distinct predictions derived for rivals
Conditions found: archived observations, reanalysis and existing model runs

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats: many summer days over 27 years at 150 sites, plus multiple model scenarios
Holds across composite vs regression methods, obs vs reanalysis-driven model and all sites; weaker in the coupled model
Relation kept as a regional regularity; future projection offered as model-based estimate

end.claim: Summer daily PM2.5 across US IMPROVE sites (1988–2014) and CESM simulations is positively correlated with nearby anticyclonic wave activity, most strongly in the Midwest, with higher PM2.5 percentiles more sensitive to AWA (most in the Northeast).

decisive_move.sentence: Regressing daily deseasonalized PM2.5 at the sites on gridded AWA produced the positive coefficient patterns that the composites, the model runs and the all-site maps then checked.

gates.evidence: All data were pre-existing archives (IMPROVE, ERA-Interim, CCMI output); the ozone analogy (Sun et al. 2019) steered the analysis, not data acquisition. The correlation could have come out null or negative, and significance is stippled at 5%, but no rival was set against it and the future projection was compared only with the model's own simulated change. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data; the composite threshold was chosen after comparing quantiles (Fig. S1).

imports.item: PM2.5 health impacts (mortality, cardiovascular and respiratory effects) as motivation

novelty_claims.quote: However, no previous studies have investigated how wave activity can lead to changes in PM 2.5 concentrations
Such an exploration of PM 2.5 from atmospheric motion can provide new insights into understanding the mechanism of PM 2.5 changes
This study presents new perspectives to explore both the observed and simulated PM 2.5 responses to climate change.

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: (1) the high-quantile sensitivity is regularity_in_range; at AREN1 overall r is only 0.36 and the authors say most variability comes from other drivers (§3.3 ¶1). (2) The future PM2.5 increase in the western US from AWA change is a model-based projection with no stated uncertainty, checked only against the same model's simulated change, with which it disagrees in the east (§3.4 ¶6); status at most estimate_with_resolution without resolution, inference. (3) The mechanism (subsidence, stagnation, inversions) is asserted from consistency with the literature and not tested against rivals; at most best_explanation (§3.2 ¶2). The abstract's 'up to R = 0.65' does not appear in the main text, and the abstract's 'changes between current and future climates in AWA can explain up to 75 %' conflates the present-day interannual R² (§3.4 ¶1) with future change (inference). ERA-Interim covers 1991–2010 while observations span 1988–2014; the mismatch is not explained (inference). The 90th-percentile composite threshold was chosen after looking at the data (Fig. S1). Only total PM2.5 was available, so species-level mechanisms are untested (§3.4 ¶7). No review file or discussion was supplied, so the review process cannot be coded.

disagreements.support: Their projected meteorology-driven summertime PM2.5 decrease contrasts with the AWA-based increase in the west found here; the authors attribute the discrepancy to model formulation without testing it.
disagreements.quote: In contrast, Avise et al. (2009) found that changes in meteorology tend to reduce summertime PM 2.5 concentrations

disagreements.support: Tagaris et al. projected larger future PM2.5 in the Midwest, while the AWA-predicted signal here is in the western US.
disagreements.quote: These results are somewhat consistent with Tagaris et al. (2007)

disagreements.support: Their high-quantile sensitivity to temperature agrees in kind, but its regional peak lies entirely in the east, whereas the AWA quantile contrast is shown across 145 of 150 sites.
disagreements.quote: but with PM 2.5 sensitivities to temperature peaks entirely in the east due to the regionality of PM 2.5 speciation

alternatives_considered.chosen: Composite threshold at the 90th percentile of daily PM2.5
alternatives_considered.reason: The 90th-percentile composite is most similar to the regression coefficient pattern

alternatives_considered.chosen: MERRA 500 hPa height for the REFC1SD case
alternatives_considered.reason: Should be very similar since they use largely the same observations
Over the US in summer LWA is dominated by its anticyclonic component (Sun et al., 2019)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both composite AWA and regression coefficients as relationship metrics
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Composite AWA for high PM2.5 vs regression coefficients for all PM2.5
alternatives_considered.reason: The two give consistent spatial distributions, so either can be useful
